analysis.one_liner: Strips states of their power to police securities fraud by publicly traded companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have blocked state civil securities-fraud enforcement against public companies, drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal securities law so that no state could regulate securities fraud involving a company whose stock trades on a national exchange like the NYSE or Nasdaq. Every civil fraud lawsuit would have had to go to federal court, and state securities regulators — like the New York Attorney General's office, which uses its powerful Martin Act — would have been limited to cases outside those companies or to criminal cases meeting strict federal standards. The bill's stated goal was to give public companies a single uniform federal anti-fraud standard instead of a patchwork of state "blue sky" laws. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies and their executives are the direct beneficiaries. Today they can face civil fraud actions from multiple state regulators under differing state standards, and the bill's own findings say state actions create "reputational risk" and costs even when allegations are later found baseless [S3]. Removing state civil enforcement would reduce their legal exposure and the threat of parallel state investigations. Securities exchanges and the broader public-company ecosystem would also benefit from a single rulebook, at least in the short run [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Publicly traded companies and their executives

how_it_helps.text: No state law, rule, judgment, or enforcement action could regulate securities fraud with respect to a covered issuer — a company traded on the NYSE or Nasdaq (or a similar exchange) that is engaged in interstate commerce [S3].

Federal district courts would have exclusive original jurisdiction over all civil securities-fraud actions involving covered companies, and any state-court case could be removed to federal court [S3].

State securities regulators would keep authority only over non-covered securities for civil cases, and their criminal cases against covered companies would have to comply in all respects with federal fraud law requirements [S3].

The bill's findings argue that varying state standards raise costs, put U.S. public companies at a competitive disadvantage globally, and that the number of U.S. public companies (5,734 as of June 2017) has stagnated partly because of the lack of a uniform standard [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Retail and institutional investors who rely on state securities regulators as an additional cop on the beat. State enforcers like the New York Attorney General would lose the power to bring civil fraud actions against the companies whose shares most Americans own through retirement accounts. If federal enforcement resources fall short, some fraud against investors would go unprosecuted. Any private investor suit filed under state law would be moved to federal court, where shorter deadlines and stricter pleading standards make cases harder to bring.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors relying on state securities regulators

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate state civil enforcement against the largest public companies, removing a second layer of investor protection alongside the SEC — state enforcers historically have pursued frauds the SEC did not prioritize [S3].
State criminal fraud actions against covered companies would survive only if they comply in all respects with federal fraud-law requirements, narrowing even criminal state enforcement tools [S3].
The bill is titled 'Harmonization' but goes beyond aligning rules: it fully preempts state regulation of securities fraud for covered issuers rather than merely setting uniform standards [S3].

A fair objection from companies is real: parallel state investigations of the same alleged fraud can impose heavy costs and reputational harm on firms and their shareholders, including employees, even before any wrongdoing is proven [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The efficiency argument — one national fraud standard for companies that operate in every state — has a real basis, and state overlays can create duplicative burdens. But the bill's remedy is a blanket preemption, not a harmonized standard: it removes state civil enforcement entirely against companies that make up the bulk of the stock market, exactly the firms where the largest frauds have historically occurred. The state-oversight layer would disappear, and the outcome depends entirely on the SEC's enforcement priorities at any given time. Weighing that trade-off, the loss to investors outweighs the compliance savings for companies.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, it never got a hearing or vote and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Senator David Perdue (R-GA) introduced the bill in the Senate on September 6, 2018 [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which was its only action; the bill never left committee before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Investors and state securities regulators are better off: their existing authority to pursue securities fraud against public companies remains fully intact, while companies gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. David Perdue
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a hearing or vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no party-split on the merits was ever shown.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted companies listed on national exchanges from all state civil securities-fraud regulation and forced all investor fraud suits into federal court, cutting their legal exposure [S3]. Their gain comes from shedding accountability to the state-level enforcers who protect the investors who own their shares.

State securities commissions and state AGs would have lost civil enforcement power over nearly every major public company, keeping authority only over non-covered securities and narrow criminal cases matching federal law [S3]. Their enforcement is a primary protection for state investors.

industries.industry: Securities exchanges and national market operators
industries.note: A single federal standard for listed companies would lower friction for NYSE- and Nasdaq-listed firms, which the bill's findings argue could encourage more companies to list [S3]. The public benefit is speculative and depends on companies passing savings to shareholders rather than absorbing them.
